client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and honestly, I've been struggling more than I expected. I can't seem to focus on anything — work, chores, even just watching TV feels impossible because my mind keeps drifting back to her. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief has a way of catching us off guard, especially when it lingers in the quiet moments we thought would be safe. It makes complete sense that your mind keeps finding its way back to her; that's not a failure to cope, it's actually a sign of how much she meant to you. I hear a little hesitation about whether this will help, and that's okay — can you tell me a bit more about what's been the hardest part of the past month?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, the hardest part has been the evenings, when the house gets quiet and I just... sit there thinking about all the times I didn't call her back when I should have. There's this weight in my chest that won't go away, like I owe her something I can never pay back now. I guess I'm not sure talking about it will actually change any of that — like, she's still gone, and I still didn't do enough.
therapist: That weight you're describing — that sense of unfinished debt to her — is one of the most painful parts of grief, and I want you to know it's incredibly common, even when the love in a relationship was very real and very mutual. I notice you're speaking quickly, like there's a lot pressing to get out, but your voice also sounds quite soft and a little distant at the same time — I wonder if part of you is feeling something even heavier than the words are letting on right now. What do you think she would have said about how much you actually showed up for her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... she probably would have said something kind, she always did. But that's kind of the problem, isn't it? She was so generous with me that I can't trust what she would have said — like, maybe she was just protecting my feelings even then, and I'll never actually know the truth of it now.
therapist: There's something really poignant in what you just shared — you loved her generosity, and yet right now that same generosity is making it hard to trust her kindness, almost like grief is turning one of her greatest gifts into a source of doubt. I notice your voice sounds quite soft and a little subdued, like there's a sadness sitting underneath this that's hard to fully put into words. I'm curious — when you imagine that she *was* telling the truth, that her kindness toward you was genuine, what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I try to imagine that her kindness was real... I don't know, there's this brief moment where it feels almost like a relief, like I can breathe for a second. But then it crashes back down because if it was real, then losing her is even bigger, even more of a loss, and I'm not sure I can sit with that. It's almost easier to doubt her than to fully feel how much she meant to me.
therapist: What you just said takes a lot of courage and self-awareness to recognize — that doubting her is almost serving as a kind of protection, a way of keeping the full weight of the loss at a safer distance. That's not a flaw in you; it's actually your mind trying to shield you from pain that feels too big to hold all at once. I wonder, what might it look like to let yourself feel that loss just a little at a time, rather than all at once — do you think that feels possible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, what you're saying about my mind trying to protect me. But I'm not sure I even know how to feel it "a little at a time" — it's like once I start going there, I'm afraid it'll just swallow me whole and I won't be able to function. And honestly, part of me wonders if opening that door even a crack is worth it, because what does it actually change?
therapist: The fear that grief will swallow you whole if you let it in is so real and so understandable, and it makes sense that you'd want to protect yourself from that. But what you're describing — that brief moment of relief when you imagined her kindness was real — that *was* you opening the door a crack, and you're still here, still functioning, still talking to me. I wonder if that moment is actually a small piece of evidence that you might be more able to hold this than your mind is currently letting you believe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, that moment did feel different, like something loosened just a little. But I don't know if that means I can actually handle the full weight of it — that was just a small glimpse, not the whole thing. What if I let it in completely and I just fall apart, and there's no one there to help me put the pieces back together?
therapist: That fear of falling apart and being alone in it — that's such a vulnerable and important thing to name, and I don't want to rush past it. I notice your voice sounds a little higher and quicker, like there's an urgency underneath this, almost as if part of you is bracing for something. I want to gently ask — when you imagine falling apart, who do you picture not being there, and is it possible that fear is also connected to losing her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah... I think it's her. I mean, she's the one I'd call if things got really bad, and now I don't even know if I can do that anymore. And that's the part that scares me most — not just losing the friendship, but losing the person who was supposed to be my safety net.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — you're not only grieving her as your grandmother, but as the person who made you feel safe when the world got hard, and that's a profound double loss. It makes so much sense that the evenings feel unbearable, because that's exactly when you'd reach for that safety net and find it gone. I want to sit with that with you for a moment — in her absence, what do you think she would have wanted you to reach for when things get really hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've been sitting with that question and... honestly, it makes me tear up a little, because I know exactly what she'd say. She'd tell me to call someone, to not sit alone with it, that people need people. But that's the part that feels impossible now, because she was the only one I ever really felt comfortable calling, and everyone else just feels like... I don't know, like I'd be bothering them or they wouldn't really get it.
therapist: You already know what she'd say, and somewhere inside you, you believe it too — that's her wisdom still living in you, even now. And I notice as you said it, your voice got quite soft, like that truth is tender and a little fragile right now. I wonder if the belief that you'd be "bothering" people is something worth gently questioning — because is that your truth, or is it a story that's keeping you isolated in exactly the way she would have hated for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think you're right that it's probably a story more than the truth, but knowing that doesn't make it feel any less real when I'm actually in the moment and thinking about calling someone. It's like my head can follow the logic, but then there's this other part of me that just... freezes, and the old feeling wins anyway. And honestly, part of me wonders if reaching out would just remind me of how much has changed since she died, how the friendships aren't quite the same without her in the middle of them.
therapist: That gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of being human, and it doesn't mean the logic is wrong — it just means the emotional part of you needs more time and repetition to catch up. What you said about friendships feeling different without her at the center is really important though, because it sounds like she wasn't just your safety net, she was also part of the glue that made other connections feel possible. I'm wondering — is there one person in your life right now who she would have trusted, someone she would have pointed you toward if she could?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I've been sitting with that question and honestly... my mind went straight to her friend Carla, someone they'd known since college who was always kind to me at gatherings. But the thought of reaching out to Carla feels almost like a betrayal somehow, like I'd be trying to replace my mom or use her connection in a way that isn't really mine. I don't even know if Carla would want to hear from me, or if I'd just be this sad reminder of someone she lost too.
therapist: Carla came to mind immediately — that's worth paying attention to, because your instincts brought you straight to someone your grandmother trusted and who was kind to you. I want to gently turn the "betrayal" idea over a little, because I wonder if reaching out to Carla might actually be honoring the connection rather than exploiting it — and that Carla, who is also grieving, might find some comfort in hearing from someone who loved her too. What do you think your grandmother would have made of the two of you finding each other in this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
